what_it_does: Checking whether a chip design is correct before it is manufactured is extremely time-consuming. One key bottleneck is managing a long list of 'proof obligations' — states of the circuit that the verification tool needs to prove can never actually be reached. This paper introduces the idea of 'Critical Proof Obligations' (CPOs): a way to rank those states so that the tool focuses first on the ones most likely to unlock progress, similar to prioritizing the most-load-bearing bricks when inspecting a wall. Two techniques built on top of this idea — one that trims redundant constraints to the smallest useful set, and one that reuses discovered facts to accelerate how the tool refines its model — together reduce the overall time needed to formally verify hardware correctness.
